answer: I used the standard 2-qubit form of H2 (STO-3G, bond length 0.735 angstrom). Its energy is a sum of a few simple measurements: Z0, Z1, Z0Z1 and X0X1, plus a fixed nuclear repulsion of 0.71997 hartree. The exact ground state energy, found by diagonalizing the matrix, is -1.13731 hartree (total energy, including nuclear repulsion). For the variational method I used a one-parameter circuit (X on qubit 0, Ry(theta) on qubit 1, then a CNOT). It makes a mix of the states 01 and 10. I tried 721 settings of theta on a simulator, kept the best, and refined it. The best theta was -0.2235 rad. It gives -1.13731 hartree, which matches the exact answer to better than 1e-9 hartree. This is because the circuit can represent the true ground state of this model exactly. The principle is the variational principle: any trial state has energy at or above the true minimum, so you lower the energy by tuning the circuit and keep the lowest. I then submitted both measurement circuits as one job on garnet:mock (job 01a16062-480f-7506-955b-a5ea36d751e7, 1000 shots each). One circuit measures in the Z basis, and one adds Hadamards to measure in the X basis. The mock device returns near-uniform random counts (about 250 of each bitstring) and does not simulate the circuit. So the energy computed from those counts is -0.320 hartree, far from the exact value. That gap comes from the mock, not from the method. On a real QPU the counts would follow the circuit, and the measured energy would be close to -1.137, with some error from hardware noise. I did not spend any real QPU credits.
